The Intropy model - Intropy Skip to content ## The Intropy model¶ Intropy organises every integration around two primitives: Blocks and Blueprints. Once you see how the two relate, the rest of the documentation falls into place. If you'd rather see code first, do the Quick start and come back here. ## Overview¶ A Block is the smallest independently deployable unit. Each Block has one type and one job (an Extractor pulls records from a source, a Loader writes them to a destination) and runs as its own component with its own internal pipeline. A Blueprint is a named composition of two or more Blocks, describing a complete integration end-to-end. Recurring Blueprint shapes (Golden Record, Distribution…) are named and documented, so most new integrations start from a proven shape instead of a blank page. flowchart TD E1[Extractor
source A]:::block E2[Extractor
source B]:::block R[Reconciler]:::block L1[Loader
destination A]:::block L2[Loader
destination B]:::block E1 --> R E2 --> R R --> L1 R --> L2 classDef block fill:#1e1a2e,stroke:#8066FF,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#e6e1f5; The diagram above is the Golden Record Blueprint. Each box is a Block, deployed as its own component; the arrows are the record flow between them, declared by the Blueprint. ## Blocks¶ A Block is an independently deployable component, versioned and scaled on its own. A Block typically consists of a processing pipeline (steps such as Deserialize, Validate, Transform, Serialize) and exchanges records with other Blocks through the wiring the Blueprint declares. Every Block has exactly one type, and each type has one narrow job. These are the Block types the framework ships today: | Block type | Job | Extractor | Pull records from a source system | Reconciler | Match and merge records that describe the same entity across sources | Assembler | Compose the canonical output shape from reconciled records | Loader | Write records to a destination system | Transactional Integration | Move records from a source system to a destination system as one atomic flow Blocks compose freely: a Blueprint can wire together any combination of Blocks the integration calls for, and no type is mandatory. A one-source, one-destination integration is just Extractor → Loader. You add a Reconciler when records about the same entity arrive from multiple sources, and an Assembler when the canonical output shape needs to be composed from those reconciled records. When the flow carries transactional data (orders, postings) rather than master data, a single Transactional Integration Block covers the whole source-to-destination flow on its own. ## Edge Blocks and core Blocks¶ Every Block type belongs to one of two groups, and the split carries the failure model. A new Block type doesn't change the model — it lands in one of these two groups. An edge Block sits at the boundary to an external system. Its job is translation: it absorbs that system's data shapes, protocols, and quirks so nothing downstream has to know the system exists (in DDD terms, an anti-corruption layer). Extractors and Loaders are edge Blocks: Extractors face systems you receive data from, Loaders face systems you deliver data to. So is a Transactional Integration, which faces both at once: even though it is an end-to-end flow from source to destination, everything it does is boundary work against systems you don't control, which is exactly what makes a Block an edge Block. Because edge Blocks deal with systems you don't control, failure there is an expected condition: the source is down, credentials expired, a record violates a business rule. Edge Blocks handle these with retries, dead-letter queues, and business incidents. A core Block owns the integration's domain model. Reconcilers and Assemblers are core Blocks: both work entirely in that model, on the integration's own representation of its entities. Any translation to or from an external system's shapes belongs to an edge Block, so a core Block only ever sees records that an edge Block has already validated and normalised. Invalid input in a core Block is therefore an integration bug, not an operational condition. That failure is a technical incident that pages someone. ## Blueprints¶ A Blueprint is a named composition of two or more Blocks: it declares which Blocks make up the integration and how records flow between them. Blueprints are versioned, reviewable, and runnable in isolation against any environment. Recurring Blueprint shapes have names. When a new requirement comes in, the first question is whether it matches one of these; if it does, you scaffold and estimate against it instead of designing from scratch. When nothing matches, you compose Blocks directly, in whatever arrangement the integration needs. The named shapes are a shortcut, not a requirement. | Blueprint | Composition | Use when | Golden Record | multiple Extractors → Reconciler → multiple Loaders | Several systems hold partial or conflicting views of the same entity, and every system should receive the merged truth (the Overview diagram) | Distribution | Extractor → multiple Loaders | One system owns the data and several others need a copy; no merging, each destination gets the records in its own shape Back to top

Explore the Go CLI repo at /Users/robinhultman/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-cli (be thorough). I'm auditing terminology consistency against the official Intropy docs vocabulary.

The canonical docs vocabulary is:
- "Block" and "Blueprint" as the two primitives (capitalized in prose)
- Block types: Extractor, Reconciler, Assembler, Loader, Transactional Integration
- "edge Block" vs "core Block" grouping
- Named Blueprint shapes: "Golden Record", "Distribution" (docs mention these two; docs do NOT mention "point-to-point")
- Block internal pipeline steps: Deserialize, Validate, Transform, Serialize
- The thing that flows between Blocks is "records"
- Blocks are "components", "independently deployable"
- Docs use British spelling in prose (organise, normalise) — note which spelling the CLI uses in user-facing text

# Align intropy-cli terminology with the Intropy model docs

## Context

The docs page https://docs.intropy.io/concepts/intropy-model/ defines the canonical vocabulary: **Block** and **Blueprint** as the two capitalized primitives; Block types **Extractor, Reconciler, Assembler, Loader, Transactional Integration**; named Blueprint shapes **Golden Record** and **Distribution**; **records** as the thing that flows; internal pipeline steps **Deserialize, Validate, Transform, Serialize**.

A terminology audit of the CLI found the repo is mostly consistent — "integration" is itself a docs word ("a Blueprint … describ[es] a complete integration end-to-end"), and the loudest divergences (message vs record, "integration component") live in untracked scaffold output whose text originates in the **blueprints repo**, not here. The genuine CLI-repo issue: **"blueprint" is lowercase in every piece of prose** (help text, flag descriptions, README, CONTRIBUTING — ~all occurrences), while docs treat "Blueprint" as a proper-noun primitive.

Decisions made with Robin:
- **Keep `kind: Template` / `template.yaml`** — the Backstage mirroring is deliberate (`internal/blueprint/manifest.go:15-17`); treat as a known, intentional exception. No manifest changes.
- **Capitalize "Blueprint" in prose**; lowercase stays for arg placeholders, flag names, identifiers, and Go error strings.
- **Scope = this CLI repo now**, plus a follow-up checklist for cross-repo fixes.

## Changes

### 1. Capitalize "Blueprint" in user-facing prose

Rule: capitalize in cobra `Short`/`Long`/`Example` text, flag usage strings, interactive prompt text, and README/CONTRIBUTING prose. Do **not** change:
- arg placeholders / `Use` lines (`create <blueprint>`)
- Go error strings (idiomatically lowercase — `internal/blueprint/create.go:198-202` etc. stay as-is)
- code identifiers, JSON/YAML keys, paths, and the `blueprints/` directory name in the library repo (literal ref)

Files (find the full set with `grep -rn 'blueprint' cmd/ internal/ README.md CONTRIBUTING.md`, then apply the rule to prose hits only):
- `cmd/intropy/int_create.go` — `Short`, `Long` (line 31: "…from the official Intropy Blueprints library. The positional argument selects which Blueprint subdirectory…"), flag help at lines 87–88
- `cmd/intropy/int_describe.go` — `Short: "Describe an Intropy Blueprint"`, `Long` at line 23
- any other cobra commands / completion help mentioning blueprint in prose
- `internal/blueprint/` — interactive prompt/user-visible output strings only (not errors, not comments — comments may be updated where cheap but are not the goal)
- `README.md` (~14 prose occurrences), `CONTRIBUTING.md`

### 2. No other CLI text changes

Committed CLI source does not use "message", "flow", "point-to-point", or block-type names incorrectly — nothing else to fix here. Untracked dirs (`Orders/`, `Demo/`, `benchmark/`, `tmp/`) are generated/benchmark artifacts and are not edited.

## Implementation notes

- Invoke the `golang-cli` skill before editing cobra help text (house rule).
- This is a docs/UX-only change; no behavior changes, no new tests needed beyond keeping existing ones green (some tests may assert on help/prompt strings — update those assertions if they break).

## Verification

1. `go build ./... && go test ./...`
2. `go run ./cmd/intropy int create --help` and `int describe --help` — eyeball capitalized "Blueprint" in prose, lowercase `<blueprint>` placeholder intact.
3. `grep -rn 'blueprint' cmd/ internal/ README.md CONTRIBUTING.md` — remaining lowercase hits should only be identifiers, `Use:` placeholders, error strings, paths.
4. Suggest a commit point after verification (do not auto-commit).

## Follow-ups (other repos — not done in this change)

- **blueprints repo (template text that ends up in scaffolded projects):**
  - "message"/"messages" → "record(s)" in generated README/AGENTS text (docs: records flow between Blocks)
  - "integration component" → align with docs ("Block" is the deployable component; an "integration" is what a Blueprint describes)
  - Scaffolded pipeline adds a fifth `Send` step; docs list only Deserialize/Validate/Transform/Serialize as the internal steps — align docs or template wording
- **backstage-scaffold skill:** still advertises "point-to-point" — the docs page no longer uses that term (the concept is now the "Transactional Integration" Block type). Also check `golden-record`/`distribution` labels render as "Golden Record"/"Distribution" in user-facing text.
- **benchmark skill (`benchmark/skills/biztalk-migration-no-cli/SKILL.md`, untracked):** says "Blueprint = `Transactional`" — wrong term ("Transactional Integration") and wrong category (it's a Block type, not a Blueprint shape).
- **Spelling:** docs prose is British (organise/normalise), CLI text is American (-ize). Left as-is in the CLI (American is conventional for code/CLI text); raise with docs owners if a single convention is wanted.

# Agent Instructions

This project is an ASP.NET Minimal API integration component using Dapr pub/sub with the in-memory component. It exposes `POST /publish`, and the subscribed endpoint runs the order send pipeline, writing the result to a local storage binding.

## Project overview

- Framework: .NET 10
- App type: ASP.NET Core Minimal API
- Dapr package: `Dapr.AspNetCore`
- App id: `int89`
- App port: `5001`
- Pub/sub component: `pubsub` (in-memory)
- Topic: `messages`
- Output binding: `local-storage` (Dapr local storage, rootPath `./local/test/out`)

## Important files

- `src/Program.cs` - DI wiring and framework registration.
- `src/Configuration/Constants.cs` - component, topic, and binding names.
- `src/Ingest/Endpoints.cs` - HTTP endpoints and the Dapr subscription.
- `src/Process/` - the order send pipeline, its builder, and step classes.
- `local/dapr-components/` - local Dapr component YAMLs (pub/sub, storage binding).
- `Dockerfile` - multi-stage image build on the .NET chiseled ASP.NET runtime,
  listening on port 5001 (`docker build -t int89 .`); the image contains
  only the app — the Dapr sidecar and components come from the deployment
  environment.
- `src/INT89.http` - sample HTTP requests.

## Build and run

Build:

```bash
dotnet build ./src
```

Run with Dapr:

```bash
dapr run \
  --app-id int89 \
  --app-port 5001 \
  --dapr-http-port 3500 \
  --resources-path ./local/dapr-components \
  -- dotnet run --project ./src --urls http://localhost:5001
```

## Testing

Use `src/INT89.http` to post a sample message to `POST /publish`.

## Framework guidance

How-to knowledge for the Intropy framework (pipelines, blocks, endpoints, Dapr components, testing) lives in the Intropy skills collection under `.agents/skills/`. If it is not installed, run `intropy skills collection add --name intropy --ref harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest`.

# Adopt neutral "template" vocabulary in intropy-cli

## Context

The docs page https://docs.intropy.io/concepts/intropy-model/ defines the canonical vocabulary: **Block** and **Blueprint** as the two primitives — a Blueprint is "a named composition of **two or more Blocks**" (named shapes: Golden Record, Distribution); Block types are Extractor, Reconciler, Assembler, Loader, **Transactional Integration**.

Audit finding: the CLI calls the items in the `integrio-intropy/intropy-blueprints` repo "blueprints", but **nothing in that repo is a docs Blueprint**. The repo holds two scaffolding templates (`hello-world`, `transactional`); each renders a single component, and `transactional` is titled "Transactional Integration" — which docs classify as a **Block type**. The manifest already says `kind: Template`. So "blueprints library" currently conflates the scaffolding template with the docs primitive, and its most substantive entry is a template for the *other* primitive.

Decision (Robin): **switch CLI human-facing vocabulary to the neutral "template"**, reserving "Blueprint" strictly for the docs meaning. Repo rename and machine-readable key renames are follow-ups, not in this change. (`kind: Template` stays — already correct under this decision.)

## Changes (this repo)

### 1. Reword human-facing "blueprint" → "template"

Cobra help text:
- `cmd/intropy/int_create.go:29-31` — `Use: "create <template>"`; Long becomes e.g. "Scaffold a new integration from a template in the official Intropy template library. The positional argument selects which template subdirectory to render (e.g. 'hello-world'). …"
- `cmd/intropy/int_create.go:87-88` — `--name`: "…sets the template's 'name' parameter…"; `--version`: "template release tag (default: latest)"
- `cmd/intropy/int_describe.go:21-23,53` — `Use: "describe <template>"`, `Short: "Describe an Intropy template"`, Long: "Print the template manifest — metadata and parameter schema…", `--version` help

User-visible messages and errors in `internal/blueprint/`:
- `create.go:93` — "created %s from %s/%s@%s (template %s)"
- `create.go:125,195,198,201` — "template %q is missing skeleton/…", "template name is required", "invalid template name %q…"
- `github.go:82` — "template %q not found in %s/%s@%s"

Docs prose:
- `README.md` (~14 occurrences) and `CONTRIBUTING.md` — reword to "template"; where the repo is named, keep the literal `intropy-blueprints` and note templates live there (the repo rename is a follow-up). Where the docs primitive is genuinely meant, write capitalized "Blueprint".

Tests asserting on these strings will need matching updates (`go test ./...` will surface them).

### 2. Keep stable (deliberate non-changes)

- **Machine-readable keys**: `.intropy/scaffold.json` `"blueprint"` key (`internal/blueprint/create.go:41` — `manifests create` pins to it) and `int describe` JSON output key (`internal/blueprint/describe.go:42`). Renaming these is a schema change (bump `schemaVersion`) to do alongside the repo rename follow-up, coordinated with consumers (CI/Backstage parse JSON output).
- **Go package/identifiers**: `internal/blueprint`, `blueprint.Create`, `CreateOptions.Blueprint`, `completeBlueprints` etc. stay — internal only; rename opportunistically with the repo rename (note: bare `template` collides with `text/template` as a package name; `scaffold` is a candidate).
- **`kind: Template` / `template.yaml`** — already aligned with the new vocabulary.

### 3. Save the vocabulary decision to memory

New project memory: CLI human-facing term is "template"; "Blueprint" reserved for the docs primitive (composition of 2+ Blocks); machine keys/`intropy-blueprints` repo name unchanged pending follow-up.

## Implementation notes

- Invoke the `golang-cli` skill before editing cobra help text (house rule).
- No behavior changes. Untracked dirs (`Orders/`, `Demo/`, `benchmark/`, `tmp/`) are generated/benchmark artifacts — untouched.

## Verification

1. `go build ./... && go test ./...` (update string assertions that break).
2. `go run ./cmd/intropy int create --help` and `int describe --help` — prose says "template"; no stray "blueprint" in human-facing text.
3. `go run ./cmd/intropy int describe hello-world` (network) — describe output reads correctly; JSON output keys unchanged.
4. `grep -rni 'blueprint' cmd/ internal/ README.md CONTRIBUTING.md` — remaining hits are only: identifiers, JSON keys, the `intropy-blueprints` repo literal, and genuine docs-primitive references (capitalized).
5. Suggest a commit point after verification (no auto-commit).

## Follow-ups (separate decisions/repos — written up, not done here)

- **Repo rename**: `intropy-blueprints` → e.g. `intropy-templates`; update `defaultBlueprintRepo` (`internal/blueprint/github.go:15`), rely on GitHub redirects for old scaffold.json pins; then rename machine keys (`scaffold.json` `blueprint` → `template`, describe JSON) with a `schemaVersion` bump, and optionally the Go package.
- **Docs tension**: a single Transactional Integration Block is a complete integration but fails the "two or more Blocks" Blueprint definition — docs should either loosen the definition or explicitly state single-Block integrations have no Blueprint. Docs could also name the template library concept ("you scaffold against a shape" is the closest phrasing today).
- **blueprints repo template text** (ends up in scaffolded projects): "message(s)" → "record(s)"; "integration component" → docs-aligned wording; scaffolded pipeline's fifth `Send` step vs docs' four internal steps (Deserialize/Validate/Transform/Serialize).
- **backstage-scaffold skill**: still advertises "point-to-point" — retired in docs (now the Transactional Integration Block type); check golden-record/distribution labels render as "Golden Record"/"Distribution".
- **benchmark skill** (`benchmark/skills/biztalk-migration-no-cli/SKILL.md`, untracked): "Blueprint = `Transactional`" is wrong term and wrong category.
- **Spelling**: docs are British (organise/normalise), CLI is American (-ize) — left American here; raise with docs owners if one convention is wanted.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/robinhultman/.claude/skills/golang-cli

**Persona:** You are a Go CLI engineer. You build tools that feel native to the Unix shell — composable, scriptable, and predictable under automation.

**Modes:**

- **Build** — creating a new CLI from scratch: follow the project structure, root command setup, flag binding, and version embedding sections sequentially.
- **Extend** — adding subcommands, flags, or completions to an existing CLI: read the current command tree first, then apply changes consistent with the existing structure.
- **Review** — auditing an existing CLI for correctness: check the Common Mistakes table, verify `SilenceUsage`/`SilenceErrors`, flag-to-Viper binding, exit codes, and stdout/stderr discipline.

# Go CLI Best Practices

Use Cobra + Viper as the default stack for Go CLI applications. Cobra provides the command/subcommand/flag structure and Viper handles configuration from files, environment variables, and flags with automatic layering. This combination powers kubectl, docker, gh, hugo, and most production Go CLIs.

When using Cobra or Viper, refer to the library's official documentation and code examples for current API signatures.

For trivial single-purpose tools with no subcommands and few flags, stdlib `flag` is sufficient.

## Quick Reference

| Concern             | Package / Tool                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Commands & flags    | `github.com/spf13/cobra`             |
| Configuration       | `github.com/spf13/viper`             |
| Flag parsing        | `github.com/spf13/pflag` (via Cobra) |
| Colored output      | `github.com/fatih/color`             |
| Table output        | `github.com/olekukonko/tablewriter`  |
| Interactive prompts | `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea` |
| Version injection   | `go build -ldflags`                  |
| Distribution        | `goreleaser`                         |

## Project Structure

Organize CLI commands in `cmd/myapp/` with one file per command. Keep `main.go` minimal — it only calls `Execute()`.

```
myapp/
├── cmd/
│   └── myapp/
│       ├── main.go              # package main, only calls Execute()
│       ├── root.go              # Root command + Viper init
│       ├── serve.go             # "serve" subcommand
│       ├── migrate.go           # "migrate" subcommand
│       └── version.go           # "version" subcommand
├── go.mod
└── go.sum
```

`main.go` should be minimal — see [assets/examples/main.go](assets/examples/main.go).

## Root Command Setup

The root command initializes Viper configuration and sets up global behavior via `PersistentPreRunE`. See [assets/examples/root.go](assets/examples/root.go).

Key points:

- `SilenceUsage: true` MUST be set — prevents printing the full usage text on every error
- `SilenceErrors: true` MUST be set — lets you control error output format yourself
- `PersistentPreRunE` runs before every subcommand, so config is always initialized
- Logs go to stderr, output goes to stdout

## Subcommands

Add subcommands by creating separate files in `cmd/myapp/` and registering them in `init()`. See [assets/examples/serve.go](assets/examples/serve.go) for a complete subcommand example including command groups.

## Flags

See [assets/examples/flags.go](assets/examples/flags.go) for all flag patterns:

### Persistent vs Local

- **Persistent** flags are inherited by all subcommands (e.g., `--config`)
- **Local** flags only apply to the command they're defined on (e.g., `--port`)

### Required Flags

Use `MarkFlagRequired`, `MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive`, and `MarkFlagsOneRequired` for flag constraints.

### Flag Validation with RegisterFlagCompletionFunc

Provide completion suggestions for flag values.

### Always Bind Flags to Viper

This ensures `viper.GetInt("port")` returns the flag value, env var `MYAPP_PORT`, or config file value — whichever has highest precedence.

## Argument Validation

Cobra provides built-in validators for positional arguments. See [assets/examples/args.go](assets/examples/args.go) for both built-in and custom validation examples.

| Validator                   | Description                          |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `cobra.NoArgs`              | Fails if any args provided           |
| `cobra.ExactArgs(n)`        | Requires exactly n args              |
| `cobra.MinimumNArgs(n)`     | Requires at least n args             |
| `cobra.MaximumNArgs(n)`     | Allows at most n args                |
| `cobra.RangeArgs(min, max)` | Requires between min and max         |
| `cobra.ExactValidArgs(n)`   | Exactly n args, must be in ValidArgs |

## Configuration with Viper

Viper resolves configuration values in this order (highest to lowest precedence):

1. **CLI flags** (explicit user input)
2. **Environment variables** (deployment config)
3. **Config file** (persistent settings)
4. **Defaults** (set in code)

See [assets/examples/config.go](assets/examples/config.go) for complete Viper integration including struct unmarshaling and config file watching.

### Example Config File (.myapp.yaml)

```yaml
port: 8080
host: localhost
log-level: info
database:
  dsn: postgres://localhost:5432/myapp
  max-conn: 25
```

With the setup above, these are all equivalent:

- Flag: `--port 9090`
- Env var: `MYAPP_PORT=9090`
- Config file: `port: 9090`

## Version and Build Info

Version SHOULD be embedded at compile time using `ldflags`. See [assets/examples/version.go](assets/examples/version.go) for the version command and build instructions.

## Exit Codes

Exit codes MUST follow Unix conventions:

| Code  | Meaning           | When to Use                               |
| ----- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| 0     | Success           | Operation completed normally              |
| 1     | General error     | Runtime failure                           |
| 2     | Usage error       | Invalid flags or arguments                |
| 64-78 | BSD sysexits      | Specific error categories                 |
| 126   | Cannot execute    | Permission denied                         |
| 127   | Command not found | Missing dependency                        |
| 128+N | Signal N          | Terminated by signal (e.g., 130 = SIGINT) |

See [assets/examples/exit_codes.go](assets/examples/exit_codes.go) for a pattern mapping errors to exit codes.

## I/O Patterns

See [assets/examples/output.go](assets/examples/output.go) for all I/O patterns:

- **stdout vs stderr**: NEVER write diagnostic output to stdout — stdout is for program output (pipeable), stderr for logs/errors/diagnostics
- **Detecting pipe vs terminal**: check `os.ModeCharDevice` on stdout
- **Machine-readable output**: support `--output` flag for table/json/plain formats
- **Colors**: use `fatih/color` which auto-disables when output is not a terminal

## Signal Handling

Signal handling MUST use `signal.NotifyContext` to propagate cancellation through context. See [assets/examples/signal.go](assets/examples/signal.go) for graceful HTTP server shutdown.

## Shell Completions

Cobra generates completions for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell automatically. See [assets/examples/completion.go](assets/examples/completion.go) for both the completion command and custom flag/argument completions.

## Testing CLI Commands

Test commands by executing them programmatically and capturing output. See [assets/examples/cli_test.go](assets/examples/cli_test.go).

Use `cmd.OutOrStdout()` and `cmd.ErrOrStderr()` in commands (instead of `os.Stdout` / `os.Stderr`) so output can be captured in tests.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Writing to `os.Stdout` directly | Tests can't capture output. Use `cmd.OutOrStdout()` which tests can redirect to a buffer |
| Calling `os.Exit()` inside `RunE` | Cobra's error handling, deferred functions, and cleanup code never run. Return an error, let `main()` decide |
| Not binding flags to Viper | Flags won't be configurable via env/config. Call `viper.BindPFlag` for every configurable flag |
| Missing `viper.SetEnvPrefix` | `PORT` collides with other tools. Use a prefix (`MYAPP_PORT`) to namespace env vars |
| Logging to stdout | Unix pipes chain stdout — logs corrupt the data stream for the next program. Logs go to stderr |
| Printing usage on every error | Full help text on every error is noise. Set `SilenceUsage: true`, save full usage for `--help` |
| Config file required | Users without a config file get a crash. Ignore `viper.ConfigFileNotFoundError` — config should be optional |
| Not using `PersistentPreRunE` | Config initialization must happen before any subcommand. Use root's `PersistentPreRunE` |
| Hardcoded version string | Version gets out of sync with tags. Inject via `ldflags` at build time from git tags |
| Not supporting `--output` format | Scripts can't parse human-readable output. Add JSON/table/plain for machine consumption |

## Related Skills

See `samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-project-layout`, `samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-dependency-injection`, `samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-testing`, `samber/cc-skills-golang@golang-design-patterns` skills.

# intropy CLI

`intropy` is the command-line interface for working with Intropy integrations
and agent skills. It does two things:

- **Scaffolds integrations** from the official Intropy blueprint library hosted at
  [`integrio-intropy/intropy-blueprints`](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-blueprints).
- **Manages agent skills** as OCI artifacts — adding, listing, updating, and
  publishing skills (individually or as curated collections) against any OCI
  registry. The skills subsystem implements the
  [Agent Skills OCI Artifacts Spec](https://github.com/ThomasVitale/agents-skills-oci-artifacts-spec),
  so artifacts published with `intropy skills publish` interoperate with any
  other spec-compliant tooling.

## Install

### Homebrew (macOS)

Distributed as a Homebrew cask (macOS only):

```sh
brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
brew install intropy
```

The `brew trust` step is required when `HOMEBREW_REQUIRE_TAP_TRUST` is set —
the default on current Homebrew (6.x+). On older versions without that
requirement you can skip it.

# Contributing to intropy CLI

Thank you for your interest in contributing! This document covers the workflow,
standards, and conventions we follow.

## Table of Contents

- [Getting Started](#getting-started)
- [Development Workflow](#development-workflow)
- [Commit Message Convention](#commit-message-convention)
- [Pull Request Process](#pull-request-process)
- [Code Standards](#code-standards)
- [Testing](#testing)
- [Project Conventions](#project-conventions)
- [Reporting Issues](#reporting-issues)

---

## Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- [Go 1.26+](https://go.dev/dl/)
- macOS or Linux (Windows developers: use [WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install))
- A working Go module cache (`go env GOPATH`)

### Clone and build

```bash
git clone https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli.git
cd intropy-cli
make build
```

Or manually:

```bash
go build -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
```

Verify the build:

```bash
./bin/intropy version
# or
make run ARGS="version"
```

## Development Workflow

We use a **feature-branch workflow** with pull requests to `main`.

```bash
# Sync your fork
gh repo sync --branch main

# Or manually
git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main

# Create a feature branch
git checkout -b feat/short-description
```

### Branch naming

| Prefix | Use for |
|--------|---------|
| `feat/` | New commands, flags, or capabilities |
| `fix/` | Bug fixes |
| `docs/` | README, help text, or code comment changes |
| `refactor/` | Internal restructuring without behavior change |
| `test/` | New or updated tests |
| `chore/` | Dependency updates, tooling, maintenance |

**Examples:** `feat/int-create-dry-run`, `fix/blueprint-archive-paths`, `docs/readme-install`

## Commit Message Convention

We follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) for
automated changelog generation.

```
<type>(<scope>): <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]
```

**Types:** `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`

**Scopes (common):** `int`, `skills`, `oci`, `blueprint`, `cli`, `deps`

**Examples:**

```
feat(int): add --dry-run flag to create

fix(blueprint): handle nested archive paths on extraction

docs(readme): update install instructions for macOS
```

## Pull Request Process

1. **Open a draft PR early** for large or complex changes.
2. **Fill out the PR description** — what changed and why.
3. **Ensure CI passes** — `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `gofmt` must be green.
4. **Request review** from maintainers.
5. **Address feedback** promptly. Amend commits and force-push to the same branch.

### PR Checklist

- [ ] `make check` passes (fmt, vet, tests)
- [ ] `make ci` passes if you have `golangci-lint` installed (full pipeline)
- [ ] Code is formatted with `gofmt` (or `gofumpt`)
- [ ] `go mod tidy` has been run if imports changed
- [ ] New or changed behavior has tests
- [ ] Command-line changes update help text and README if applicable
- [ ] Commit messages follow the convention above
- [ ] Only relevant files are committed (no `git add .`)
- [ ] No debug code, `fmt.Printf` artifacts, or temporary files

## Code Standards

### Go style

- Follow [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go) and the
  [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments).
- Run `make fmt` (or `gofumpt`) before committing.
- Run `make vet` to catch common mistakes.
- Run `make tidy` after adding or removing imports.

### CLI patterns

This project uses Cobra + Viper. When adding or modifying commands:

- Set `SilenceUsage: true` and `SilenceErrors: true` on the command.
- Return errors from `RunE` — never call `os.Exit()` inside commands.
- Write diagnostic output to `cmd.ErrOrStderr()`, program output to `cmd.OutOrStdout()`.
- Bind flags to Viper with `viper.BindPFlag` for env/config support.
- Use `cobra.ExactArgs`, `cobra.MinimumNArgs`, etc. for argument validation.
- Provide `RegisterFlagCompletionFunc` for flag value completion.

### Error handling

- Return wrapped errors with context: `fmt.Errorf("resolving blueprint: %w", err)`
- Use exit code `2` for usage errors (invalid flags/args), `1` for runtime errors.

## Testing

### Run the test suite

```bash
make test
```

Or manually:

```bash
go test ./...
```

### Run with race detection

```bash
make test-race
```

Or manually:

```bash
go test -race ./...
```

### Key testing patterns

- Test commands by executing them programmatically and capturing output.
- Use `cmd.SetOut(buf)` and `cmd.SetErr(errBuf)` so tests can inspect output.
- Mock OCI registry calls and HTTP transports (e.g. the GitHub blueprint client) — do not hit the network or real registries in tests.
- Each `_test.go` file lives alongside the code it tests.

### Adding tests

- New features **must** include tests.
- Bug fixes **should** include a regression test.
- Table-driven tests are preferred for multiple cases.

## Project Conventions

### Project layout

```
cmd/intropy/         Cobra commands — one file per command + tests
internal/blueprint/  Blueprint download, validation, describe, render
internal/skill/      skills.json/lockfile, install/update/add, collection cache
internal/skill/oci/  OCI client wrappers, pack/push/pull, references
```

### Version stamping

Version, commit, and build date are injected at compile time. When testing locally:

```bash
go build -ldflags "\
  -X main.version=dev \
  -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
  -X main.date=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
  -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
```

### OCI and skills compliance

The `skills` subsystem implements the
[Agent Skills OCI Artifacts Spec](https://github.com/ThomasVitale/agents-skills-oci-artifacts-spec).
When modifying OCI packaging, pulling, or metadata, ensure conformance with the
spec. Changes that affect wire format or artifact structure should be discussed
in an issue first.

## Reporting Issues

Before opening an issue:

1. Search existing issues (open and closed) for duplicates.
2. Use a clear, descriptive title.

A good bug report includes:
- Steps to reproduce
- Expected vs. actual behavior
- Output of `intropy version`
- Environment: OS, Go version (`go version`)
- If applicable: the exact command and flags used

## License

By contributing, you agree that your contributions will be licensed under the
[MIT License](LICENSE).

## Security

If you discover a security vulnerability, **do not open a public issue**.
Email the maintainers directly.

---

Questions? Open a discussion or reach out to the maintainers.

Scaffold a new integration from the official Intropy template library. The positional argument selects which template subdirectory to render (e.g. 'hello-world'). After scaffolding, offers to install the Intropy agent skills collection into the new integration; --install-skills installs and --skip-install-skills skips without prompting, otherwise the prompt is skipped with --no-input or when stdin is not a terminal.

Usage:
  intropy int create <template> [flags]

Flags:
      --force                 allow rendering into a non-empty output directory
  -h, --help                  help for create
      --install-skills        install the Intropy agent skills collection without prompting
  -n, --name string           integration name; sets the template's 'name' parameter and, unless -o is set, becomes the output directory
      --no-input              disable interactive prompts for missing values
  -o, --output string         destination directory (defaults to --name)
      --output-json string    write a machine-readable result document to this path (- for stdout)
  -s, --set stringArray       set a value as key=value (repeatable)
      --skip-install-skills   skip the agent skills install without prompting
  -f, --values stringArray    values file in YAML/JSON (repeatable; use - to read one doc from stdin)
      --version string        template release tag (default: latest)

Global Flags:
      --no-color   disable colored output
  -q, --quiet      suppress non-error output
  -v, --verbose    enable verbose output
==== describe ====
Print the template manifest — metadata and parameter schema — for the requested release. Use --output json to emit a stable, machine-readable document (the same schema Backstage's frontend renders).

Usage:
  intropy int describe <template> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for describe
  -o, --output string    output format: plain or json (default "plain")
      --version string   template release tag (default: latest)

Global Flags:
      --no-color   disable colored output
  -q, --quiet      suppress non-error output
  -v, --verbose    enable verbose output

**What changed** (6 files):
- `cmd/intropy/int_create.go` and `int_describe.go` — `Use` placeholders are now `<template>`, and all Short/Long/flag help says "template" ("Scaffold a new integration from the official Intropy template library…").

1	# intropy CLI
2	
3	`intropy` is the command-line interface for working with Intropy integrations
4	and agent skills. It does two things:
5	
6	- **Scaffolds integrations** from the official Intropy template library hosted at
7	  [`integrio-intropy/intropy-templates`](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-templates).
8	- **Manages agent skills** as OCI artifacts — adding, listing, updating, and
9	  publishing skills (individually or as curated collections) against any OCI
10	  registry. The skills subsystem implements the
11	  [Agent Skills OCI Artifacts Spec](https://github.com/ThomasVitale/agents-skills-oci-artifacts-spec),
12	  so artifacts published with `intropy skills publish` interoperate with any
13	  other spec-compliant tooling.
14	
15	## Install
16	
17	### Homebrew (macOS)
18	
19	Distributed as a Homebrew cask (macOS only):
20	
21	```sh
22	brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
23	brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
24	brew install intropy
25	```
26	
27	The `brew trust` step is required when `HOMEBREW_REQUIRE_TAP_TRUST` is set —
28	the default on current Homebrew (6.x+). On older versions without that
29	requirement you can skip it.
30	
31	On Linux, use the quick install script below or download a binary from the
32	[releases page](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases).
33	
34	### Quick install (macOS / Linux)
35	
36	```sh
37	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
38	```
39	
40	With options:
41	
42	```sh
43	# Install to a custom prefix
44	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --prefix ~/.local
45	
46	# Install a specific version
47	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --version v1.0.0
48	```
49	
50	The script detects your OS and architecture, downloads the matching release
51	archive, verifies the SHA256 checksum, optionally verifies the cosign signature,
52	and installs the binary and shell completions.
53	
54	### Docker
55	
56	Multi-arch images (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) are published to GHCR on every
57	release, built on `distroless/static` and running as a non-root user.
58	
59	```sh
60	docker pull ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:latest
61	
62	# Scaffolding writes into the working directory: mount your project at /work
63	# and match your uid so files aren't owned by the container user
64	docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
65	  ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli int create hello-world --name Orders
66	```
67	
68	The image contains no shell — the binary is the entrypoint. Images are signed
69	with cosign; verify with:
70	
71	```sh
72	cosign verify \
73	  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli" \
74	  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
75	  ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:latest
76	```
77	
78	### From source
79	
80	Requires Go 1.26+.
81	
82	```sh
83	git clone https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli.git
84	cd intropy-cli
85	make build
86	```
87	
88	Or manually:
89	
90	```sh
91	go build -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
92	```
93	
94	Add `bin/` to your `PATH`, or move the binary somewhere on your `PATH`.
95	
96	### Verifying signatures
97	
98	Release binaries are signed with [cosign](https://sigstore.dev/) using
99	keyless signing via GitHub Actions OIDC. Each release includes `.sig` and
100	`.pem` files for every archive.
101	
102	```sh
103	# Download the archive, its .sig, and its .pem from the GitHub release
104	cosign verify-blob \
105	  --certificate intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz.pem \
106	  --signature intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz.sig \
107	  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli" \
108	  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
109	  intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz
110	```
111	
112	### Windows
113	
114	Windows is not a supported native target. Install and run `intropy` inside
115	[WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) using the Linux
116	instructions above. The CLI relies on Unix path conventions and signal handling
117	that are not tested on Windows.
118	
119	### Version stamping
120	
121	Version, commit, and build date are injected via `-ldflags` at release time:
122	
123	```sh
124	go build -ldflags "\
125	  -X main.version=$(git describe --tags --always) \
126	  -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
127	  -X main.date=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
128	  -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
129	```
130	
131	Check what you have with:
132	
133	```sh
134	intropy version
135	```
136	
137	## Quickstart
138	
139	### Scaffold your first integration
140	
141	```sh
142	# Inspect a template before you scaffold it
143	intropy int describe hello-world
144	
145	# Render it into a new directory
146	intropy int create hello-world -o ./my-integration
147	```
148	
149	### Install a skill from a collection
150	
151	```sh
152	# Register a collection (one-time)
153	intropy skills collection add --name intropy --ref harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest
154	
155	# Install a skill by name
156	intropy skills add --name intropy-getting-started
157	
158	# List what you have installed
159	intropy skills list
160	```
161	
162	## Command overview
163	
164	```
165	intropy
166	├── int                    Manage integrations
167	<<<<<<< HEAD
168	│   ├── create <template>      Scaffold a new integration from a template
169	│   └── describe <template>    Print a template's manifest and parameter schema
170	=======
171	│   ├── create <blueprint>     Scaffold a new integration from a blueprint
172	│   └── describe <blueprint>   Print a blueprint's manifest and parameter schema
173	├── manifests              Manage deployment manifests
174	│   └── create                 Generate Kubernetes manifests for a scaffolded integration
175	>>>>>>> a1901c8 (Generate manifests)
176	├── skills                 Manage Intropy skills
177	│   ├── add [ref]              Add and install a skill from an OCI registry
178	│   ├── list                   List installed skills
179	│   ├── update [name]          Reconcile an installed skill against its collection
180	│   ├── publish                Publish a skill directory to an OCI registry
181	│   └── collection             Manage registered skill collections
182	│       ├── add                    Register a collection in skills.json
183	│       ├── update <alias>         Refresh or bump a registered collection
184	│       └── publish <spec> <ref>   Publish a collection as an OCI Image Index
185	└── version                Print version information
186	```
187	
188	Run any command with `--help` for full flag documentation.
189	
190	## Integrations (`intropy int`)
191	
192	### Describe a template
193	
194	Inspect what parameters a template accepts before scaffolding it:
195	
196	```sh
197	intropy int describe hello-world
198	intropy int describe hello-world --version v1.2.0
199	intropy int describe hello-world -o json   # machine-readable; same schema Backstage renders
200	```
201	
202	Without `--version`, the latest GitHub release is used.
203	
204	### Create an integration
205	
206	```sh
207	intropy int create hello-world --output ./my-integration
208	```
209	
210	Name the integration and scaffold it in one step. `-n/--name` sets the template's
211	`name` parameter (so you're not prompted for it) and, unless `-o` is given, becomes
212	the output directory:
213	
214	```sh
215	# scaffolds into ./orders and sets name=orders
216	intropy int create hello-world -n orders
217	
218	# -o still overrides the output directory
219	intropy int create hello-world -n orders -o ./my-integration
220	```
221	
222	Provide parameter values inline, from files, or interactively:
223	
224	```sh
225	# inline
226	intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --set name=orders --set owner=team-x
227	
228	# from a values file (repeatable; use - for stdin)
229	intropy int create hello-world -o ./out -f values.yaml
230	
231	# disable interactive prompts (fail fast on missing required values)

## Deployment manifests (`intropy manifests`)

### Generate Kubernetes manifests

Run inside a scaffolded integration (any subdirectory works — the command
walks up to find `.intropy/scaffold.json`):

```sh
intropy manifests create
```

This re-fetches the blueprint at the exact version pinned in
`.intropy/scaffold.json` and renders its `manifests/` templates into a
kustomize tree:

```
deploy/
├── base/                  Deployment + Service with Dapr sidecar annotations
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   └── kustomization.yaml
└── overlays/
    ├── dev/               Dapr components for local-style backends
    └── prod/              Real-broker placeholders, secrets via secretKeyRef
```

Values recorded at scaffold time (like `name` and `appPort`) pre-fill the
matching manifest parameters, so you're only asked for what's new — typically
the container image:

```sh
# inline
intropy manifests create --set imageRepository=ghcr.io/acme/orders --set imageTag=1.0.0

# non-interactive (fail fast on missing required values)
intropy manifests create --no-input -f deploy-values.yaml

# elsewhere than deploy/, or on top of existing files
intropy manifests create -o ./k8s --force

# newer blueprint release than the one pinned at scaffold time
intropy manifests create --version v1.5.0

# machine-readable result document (consumed by chained tooling)
intropy manifests create --output-json -
```

Projects scaffolded before `.intropy/scaffold.json` existed get an error
explaining how to add the file by hand; blueprints whose pinned release
predates `manifests/` templates are told to pass `--version` with a newer
tag.

Validate the result with `kustomize build deploy/overlays/dev` (or point your
GitOps tooling at an overlay directly).

var manifestsCreateFlagValues manifestsCreateFlags

var manifestsCreateCmd = &cobra.Command{
	Use:   "create",
	Short: "Create Kubernetes manifests for a scaffolded integration",
	Long: "Generate a kustomize base + overlays tree of Kubernetes deployment manifests for a previously scaffolded integration. " +
		"Run it inside the integration project: the command walks up from the current directory to find " + blueprint.ScaffoldRelPath + ", " +
		"re-fetches the exact blueprint version recorded there, and renders its manifests/ templates. " +
		"Scaffold values (e.g. name, appPort) pre-fill matching manifest parameters; remaining required parameters are prompted for, or supplied via --set/--values.",
	Args: cobra.NoArgs,
	RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
		sets, err := blueprint.ParseSets(manifestsCreateFlagValues.sets)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		ctx, cancel := signal.NotifyContext(cmd.Context(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
		defer cancel()
		return deploy.Create(ctx, deploy.CreateOptions{
			OutputDir:  manifestsCreateFlagValues.output,
			Version:    manifestsCreateFlagValues.version,
			SetValues:  sets,
			Files:      manifestsCreateFlagValues.values,
			Force:      manifestsCreateFlagValues.force,
			NoInput:    manifestsCreateFlagValues.noInput,
			OutputJSON: manifestsCreateFlagValues.outputJSON,
			Stdin:      cmd.InOrStdin(),
			Stdout:     cmd.OutOrStdout(),
			Stderr:     cmd.ErrOrStderr(),
			UserAgent:  "intropy-cli/" + version,
		})
	},
}

func init() {
	f := manifestsCreateCmd.Flags()
	f.StringVarP(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.output, "output", "o", "", "destination directory (default: deploy, relative to the project root)")
	f.StringVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.version, "version", "", "blueprint release tag (default: the version pinned in "+blueprint.ScaffoldRelPath+")")
	f.StringArrayVarP(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.values, "values", "f", nil, "values file in YAML/JSON (repeatable; use - to read one doc from stdin)")
	f.StringArrayVarP(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.sets, "set", "s", nil, "set a value as key=value (repeatable)")
	f.BoolVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.force, "force", false, "allow rendering into a non-empty output directory")
	f.BoolVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.noInput, "no-input", false, "disable interactive prompts for missing values")
	f.StringVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.outputJSON, "output-json", "", "write a machine-readable result document to this path (- for stdout)")

package main

import (
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"

	"github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/internal/blueprint"
	"github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/internal/deploy"
	"github.com/spf13/cobra"
)

type manifestsCreateFlags struct {
	output     string
	version    string
	values     []string
	sets       []string
	force      bool
	noInput    bool
	outputJSON string
}

var manifestsCreateFlagValues manifestsCreateFlags

var manifestsCreateCmd = &cobra.Command{
	Use:   "create",
	Short: "Create Kubernetes manifests for a scaffolded integration",
	Long: "Generate a kustomize base + overlays tree of Kubernetes deployment manifests for a previously scaffolded integration. " +
		"Run it inside the integration project: the command walks up from the current directory to find " + blueprint.ScaffoldRelPath + ", " +
		"re-fetches the exact blueprint version recorded there, and renders its manifests/ templates. " +
		"Scaffold values (e.g. name, appPort) pre-fill matching manifest parameters; remaining required parameters are prompted for, or supplied via --set/--values.",
	Args: cobra.NoArgs,
	RunE: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) error {
		sets, err := blueprint.ParseSets(manifestsCreateFlagValues.sets)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		ctx, cancel := signal.NotifyContext(cmd.Context(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
		defer cancel()
		return deploy.Create(ctx, deploy.CreateOptions{
			OutputDir:  manifestsCreateFlagValues.output,
			Version:    manifestsCreateFlagValues.version,
			SetValues:  sets,
			Files:      manifestsCreateFlagValues.values,
			Force:      manifestsCreateFlagValues.force,
			NoInput:    manifestsCreateFlagValues.noInput,
			OutputJSON: manifestsCreateFlagValues.outputJSON,
			Stdin:      cmd.InOrStdin(),
			Stdout:     cmd.OutOrStdout(),
			Stderr:     cmd.ErrOrStderr(),
			UserAgent:  "intropy-cli/" + version,
		})
	},
}

func init() {
	f := manifestsCreateCmd.Flags()
	f.StringVarP(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.output, "output", "o", "", "destination directory (default: deploy, relative to the project root)")
	f.StringVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.version, "version", "", "blueprint release tag (default: the version pinned in "+blueprint.ScaffoldRelPath+")")
	f.StringArrayVarP(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.values, "values", "f", nil, "values file in YAML/JSON (repeatable; use - to read one doc from stdin)")
	f.StringArrayVarP(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.sets, "set", "s", nil, "set a value as key=value (repeatable)")
	f.BoolVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.force, "force", false, "allow rendering into a non-empty output directory")
	f.BoolVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.noInput, "no-input", false, "disable interactive prompts for missing values")
	f.StringVar(&manifestsCreateFlagValues.outputJSON, "output-json", "", "write a machine-readable result document to this path (- for stdout)")
	manifestsCmd.AddCommand(manifestsCreateCmd)
}

1	# intropy CLI
2	
3	`intropy` is the command-line interface for working with Intropy integrations
4	and agent skills. It does two things:
5	
6	- **Scaffolds integrations** from the official Intropy template library hosted at
7	  [`integrio-intropy/intropy-templates`](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-templates).
8	- **Manages agent skills** as OCI artifacts — adding, listing, updating, and
9	  publishing skills (individually or as curated collections) against any OCI
10	  registry. The skills subsystem implements the
11	  [Agent Skills OCI Artifacts Spec](https://github.com/ThomasVitale/agents-skills-oci-artifacts-spec),
12	  so artifacts published with `intropy skills publish` interoperate with any
13	  other spec-compliant tooling.
14	
15	## Install
16	
17	### Homebrew (macOS)
18	
19	Distributed as a Homebrew cask (macOS only):
20	
21	```sh
22	brew tap integrio-intropy/tap
23	brew trust --tap integrio-intropy/tap
24	brew install intropy
25	```
26	
27	The `brew trust` step is required when `HOMEBREW_REQUIRE_TAP_TRUST` is set —
28	the default on current Homebrew (6.x+). On older versions without that
29	requirement you can skip it.
30	
31	On Linux, use the quick install script below or download a binary from the
32	[releases page](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases).
33	
34	### Quick install (macOS / Linux)
35	
36	```sh
37	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
38	```
39	
40	With options:
41	
42	```sh
43	# Install to a custom prefix
44	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --prefix ~/.local
45	
46	# Install a specific version
47	curl -fsSL https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --version v1.0.0
48	```
49	
50	The script detects your OS and architecture, downloads the matching release
51	archive, verifies the SHA256 checksum, optionally verifies the cosign signature,
52	and installs the binary and shell completions.
53	
54	### Docker
55	
56	Multi-arch images (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) are published to GHCR on every
57	release, built on `distroless/static` and running as a non-root user.
58	
59	```sh
60	docker pull ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:latest
61	
62	# Scaffolding writes into the working directory: mount your project at /work
63	# and match your uid so files aren't owned by the container user
64	docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
65	  ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli int create hello-world --name Orders
66	```
67	
68	The image contains no shell — the binary is the entrypoint. Images are signed
69	with cosign; verify with:
70	
71	```sh
72	cosign verify \
73	  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli" \
74	  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
75	  ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:latest
76	```
77	
78	### From source
79	
80	Requires Go 1.26+.
81	
82	```sh
83	git clone https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli.git
84	cd intropy-cli
85	make build
86	```
87	
88	Or manually:
89	
90	```sh
91	go build -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
92	```
93	
94	Add `bin/` to your `PATH`, or move the binary somewhere on your `PATH`.
95	
96	### Verifying signatures
97	
98	Release binaries are signed with [cosign](https://sigstore.dev/) using
99	keyless signing via GitHub Actions OIDC. Each release includes `.sig` and
100	`.pem` files for every archive.
101	
102	```sh
103	# Download the archive, its .sig, and its .pem from the GitHub release
104	cosign verify-blob \
105	  --certificate intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz.pem \
106	  --signature intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz.sig \
107	  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli" \
108	  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
109	  intropy_Darwin_arm64.tar.gz
110	```
111	
112	### Windows
113	
114	Windows is not a supported native target. Install and run `intropy` inside
115	[WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) using the Linux
116	instructions above. The CLI relies on Unix path conventions and signal handling
117	that are not tested on Windows.
118	
119	### Version stamping
120	
121	Version, commit, and build date are injected via `-ldflags` at release time:
122	
123	```sh
124	go build -ldflags "\
125	  -X main.version=$(git describe --tags --always) \
126	  -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
127	  -X main.date=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
128	  -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
129	```
130	
131	Check what you have with:
132	
133	```sh
134	intropy version
135	```
136	
137	## Quickstart
138	
139	### Scaffold your first integration
140	
141	```sh
142	# Inspect a template before you scaffold it
143	intropy int describe hello-world
144	
145	# Render it into a new directory
146	intropy int create hello-world -o ./my-integration
147	```
148	
149	### Install a skill from a collection
150	
151	```sh
152	# Register a collection (one-time)
153	intropy skills collection add --name intropy --ref harbor.intropy.io/skills/index:latest
154	
155	# Install a skill by name
156	intropy skills add --name intropy-getting-started
157	
158	# List what you have installed
159	intropy skills list
160	```
161	
162	## Command overview
163	
164	```
165	intropy
166	├── int                    Manage integrations
167	│   ├── create <template>      Scaffold a new integration from a template
168	│   └── describe <template>    Print a template's manifest and parameter schema
169	├── skills                 Manage Intropy skills
170	│   ├── add [ref]              Add and install a skill from an OCI registry
171	│   ├── list                   List installed skills
172	│   ├── update [name]          Reconcile an installed skill against its collection
173	│   ├── publish                Publish a skill directory to an OCI registry
174	│   └── collection             Manage registered skill collections
175	│       ├── add                    Register a collection in skills.json
176	│       ├── update <alias>         Refresh or bump a registered collection
177	│       └── publish <spec> <ref>   Publish a collection as an OCI Image Index
178	└── version                Print version information
179	```
180	
181	Run any command with `--help` for full flag documentation.
182	
183	## Integrations (`intropy int`)
184	
185	### Describe a template
186	
187	Inspect what parameters a template accepts before scaffolding it:
188	
189	```sh
190	intropy int describe hello-world
191	intropy int describe hello-world --version v1.2.0
192	intropy int describe hello-world -o json   # machine-readable; same schema Backstage renders
193	```
194	
195	Without `--version`, the latest GitHub release is used.
196	
197	### Create an integration
198	
199	```sh
200	intropy int create hello-world --output ./my-integration
201	```
202	
203	Name the integration and scaffold it in one step. `-n/--name` sets the template's
204	`name` parameter (so you're not prompted for it) and, unless `-o` is given, becomes
205	the output directory:
206	
207	```sh
208	# scaffolds into ./orders and sets name=orders
209	intropy int create hello-world -n orders
210	
211	# -o still overrides the output directory
212	intropy int create hello-world -n orders -o ./my-integration
213	```
214	
215	Provide parameter values inline, from files, or interactively:
216	
217	```sh
218	# inline
219	intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --set name=orders --set owner=team-x
220	
221	# from a values file (repeatable; use - for stdin)
222	intropy int create hello-world -o ./out -f values.yaml
223	
224	# disable interactive prompts (fail fast on missing required values)
225	intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --no-input -f values.yaml
226	
227	# write a machine-readable result document (consumed by chained scaffolders)
228	intropy int create hello-world -o ./out --output-json result.json
229	```
230	
231	Use `--force` to render into a non-empty directory.
232	
233	After scaffolding, `int create` offers to install the Intropy agent skills

# Backstage Scaffolder Module: intropy

A [Backstage](https://backstage.io) scaffolder backend module that provides the
`intropy:int:create` action for scaffolding integrations from
[intropy](https://github.com/integrio-intropy) blueprints.

The action shells out to the `intropy` CLI inside the scaffolder workspace, so the
CLI remains the single source of scaffolding logic. The module adapts it to the
Backstage scaffolder: workspace-relative paths, structured errors, and registered
outputs.

## Installation

Add the package to your Backstage backend:

```bash
yarn --cwd packages/backend add @intropy/backstage-plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-intropy
```

Register the module in `packages/backend/src/index.ts`:

```ts
backend.add(
  import('@intropy/backstage-plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-intropy'),
);
```

## Runtime requirement: the intropy CLI

The action runs the `intropy` binary, so it must be available in the environment
where the scaffolder backend runs. In a container image, copy it from the CLI
image:

```dockerfile
ARG INTROPY_CLI_VERSION=v0.5.0
FROM ghcr.io/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli:${INTROPY_CLI_VERSION} AS intropy-cli

# ... in the runtime stage:
COPY --from=intropy-cli /usr/local/bin/intropy /usr/local/bin/intropy
```

By default the action invokes `intropy` from `PATH`. To point at a specific
binary (useful for local development), set the optional app-config:

```yaml
intropy:
  cli:
    path: /path/to/intropy
```

## Usage in a template

```yaml
steps:
  - id: create
    action: intropy:int:create
    input:
      blueprint: hello-world
      name: MyApi
      targetPath: ./output/integrations/my-api
      values:
        someBlueprintParam: value
```

### Inputs

| Name         | Type   | Required | Description                                                          |
| ------------ | ------ | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `blueprint`  | string | yes      | Blueprint id, e.g. `hello-world`                                     |
| `name`       | string | yes      | Name of the integration to create                                    |
| `targetPath` | string | no       | Workspace-relative directory to generate into (defaults to the root) |
| `values`     | object | no       | Blueprint parameter values (may be nested)                           |

### Outputs

| Name               | Description                                          |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `outputDir`        | Workspace-relative path of the generated integration |
| `blueprintVersion` | Resolved blueprint version                           |
| `blueprint`        | Resolved blueprint id                                |

Downloading blueprints from GitHub may require an authenticated `GITHUB_TOKEN`
in the backend environment (to avoid rate limits, or when the blueprint
repository is private).

## Development

```bash
yarn install
yarn tsc
yarn test
yarn build
```

## License

Apache-2.0

Decided 2026-07-15 after auditing against https://docs.intropy.io/concepts/intropy-model/: the docs define **Blueprint** as a named composition of **two or more Blocks** (shapes: Golden Record, Distribution) and **Transactional Integration** as a *Block type*. The `intropy-blueprints` repo holds single-component scaffolding templates (`hello-world` → metadata name `dapr-minimal-api`, `transactional`), so none of its entries is a docs-valid Blueprint.

Resolution: intropy-cli human-facing text (help, errors, README, CONTRIBUTING) says **"template"**; "Blueprint" is reserved strictly for the docs meaning. Kept stable on purpose: `kind: Template`/`template.yaml`, machine-readable `"blueprint"` keys in `.intropy/scaffold.json` (see [[scaffold-json-record]]) and `int describe` JSON, the Go package `internal/blueprint`, and the repo name `intropy-blueprints`.

Open follow-ups: repo rename — Robin decided 2026-07-15 to do it now while there are ~no users; safe for old CLI versions because GitHub API 301-redirects renamed repos to the immutable repo-ID URL and the CLI's Go default client follows them (verified against docker/docker→moby/moby). Hard rule: never reoccupy the `intropy-blueprints` name or the redirect dies. Cut a CLI release updating `defaultBlueprintRepo` right after (then bump scaffold.json schemaVersion and rename machine keys); docs must resolve that a single Transactional Integration Block is a complete integration yet fails the "two or more Blocks" Blueprint definition; blueprints-repo template text says "message"/"integration component" where docs say "record"/Block; backstage-scaffold skill still advertises the retired "point-to-point" shape. Docs prose is British English (organise/normalise); CLI stays American.

All four pieces are done and verified. Here's where everything stands:

**intropy-cli `main`** — two local commits, not yet pushed:
- `0220120` — the "template" vocabulary in all human-facing text (from earlier).
- `b4714f5` — `defaultBlueprintRepo` → `intropy-templates`, README links updated, and the breaking JSON key rename: `--output-json` and `int describe -o json` now emit `"template"` instead of `"blueprint"`. The `defaults_test.go` pin and the JSON-contract tests were updated deliberately. Verified live: `int describe hello-world` fetches from `intropy-templates` directly, and old binaries keep working via GitHub's 301 redirect (confirmed the redirect resolves `releases/latest` correctly).

**`feature/manifests` branch** — rebased onto the new main (one README conflict, resolved) plus commit `bfc47fb`: `scaffold.json` and the manifests `--output-json` now use a `"template"` key while **schemaVersion stays 1**, since the schema never shipped — no version bump will ever be needed. End-to-end verified: scaffolding `hello-world` writes `{"schemaVersion": 1, "template": "hello-world", "repo": "intropy-templates", ...}` and `manifests create` reads it back correctly (it errors helpfully because v0.1.6 has no `manifests/` dir yet — the known blueprints-repo follow-up).

**Backstage scaffolder module** — [PR #1](https://github.com/integrio-intropy/scaffolder-backend-module-intropy/pull/1) opened: action input `blueprint` → `template`, outputs → `templateVersion`/`template`, and the CLI result parser accepts both keys so pre-rename CLI binaries still work (new test covers this). Typecheck clean, 10/10 tests pass. Code search found no in-org callers of the action, so the hard rename is safe — but any future Backstage template YAML must use `input.template`.

**One heads-up**: the `hello-world` directory's manifest declares `metadata.name: dapr-minimal-api` — directory and manifest name disagree, worth a cleanup in `intropy-templates`.

**What's left is the outward part, ready when you are**: push the two commits on `main`, then tag the release — latest is `v1.0.2`, and since the JSON key rename is breaking I'd tag `v2.0.0` (or `v1.1.0` if you treat the pre-1.x-style "no users" stance as license to minor-bump). `git push origin main && git tag v2.0.0 && git push origin v2.0.0` should trigger the release pipeline. Say the word and I'll run it.
